title: "Families of safety officers killed in line of duty to receive ongoing benefits following Coeur d’Alene firefighter ambush"

BOISE — Gov. Brad Little joined firefighters, police and affected families from across the state at the Idaho Fallen Firefighters Memorial Park on Tuesday to sign into law a new death benefit for families of public safety officers killed in the line of duty.

The law arrives less than a year after battalion chief Frank Harwood of Kootenai County Fire and Rescue and battalion chief John Morrison of the Coeur d’Alene Fire Department were [killed by a gunman](https://cdapress.com/news/2025/jun/30/suspect-ambushed-firefighters-move-vehicle) on Coeur d’Alene’s Canfield Mountain on June 29, 2025.

Matthew Smith, vice president of the Professional Firefighters of Idaho, described the legislation as a “step forward” in Idaho’s support for public safety officers and their families. For public officers in the state, HB 642 closes the gap between injury and death benefits, providing “meaningful support and peace” for families of officers who have given everything in service of Idaho, Smith said.

During the ceremony attended by surviving family members of public safety officers, Smith said the legislation ensures the sacrifices of Harwood, Morrison, Ada County Sheriff Deputy Tobin Bolter and Caldwell Fire Deputy Chief Brad Trosky-Johnson would have a lasting impact on current and future fire and police officers in Idaho.

Bolter, at 27 years old, was shot on April 20, 2024 during a Boise traffic stop and succumbed to his injuries after being taken to the hospital. He was the first sheriff deputy in the county be killed in the line of duty, as was previously reported by the [Associated Press](https://www.idahopress.com/news/local/ada-county-deputy-dies-after-being-shot-during-boise-traffic-stop/article_d2e041a0-fffc-11ee-a763-0b478e97a320.html).

Trosky-Johnson was [recognized at the Idaho Fallen Firefighters Memorial](https://www.idahopress.com/news/local/courage-once-had-a-heartbeat-caldwell-deputy-chiefs-name-added-to-idaho-fallen-firefighters-memorial/article_151442c6-4e8e-4f2f-9f19-ed6b469690eb.html) last year after dying suddenly at the age of 55 after suffering a medical emergency the Public Safety Officers’ Benefit (PSOB) Office found to have been in the line of duty.

“This legislation ensures their legacy will endure,” Smith said. “It stands as a lasting promise, written into law, that their families will be cared for, and that we — as a community, as a brotherhood and sisterhood — will continue to stand together in their memory and their honor.”

In his remarks, Little expressed gratitude for the legislature honoring and compensating the first responders who have made sacrifices for Idahoans along with their families.

”The families are such an integral part of it,” Little said. “There’s very few people in public safety that don’t have a strong family and friends around them.”

Pete Holley, fire chief for Kootenai County Fire & Rescue, said the past legislation treated deaths in the line of duty as if the person “retired the day before they died,” meaning families would be eligible for a retirement benefit, but not the one-time and ongoing benefits associated with injury in the line of duty. By signing the amended legislation into law, Holley said the intent of the previous legislation will finally be fully realized.

“I spoke with Mrs. Harwood and this doesn’t lighten her loss,” Holley said. “It doesn’t do anything to make the events on Canfield any easier to navigate, but it reduces the level of uncertainty as you navigate the future.”

The new law amends SB 1096, which passed in 2021 and established a new benefit under the Public Employee Retirement System of Idaho (PERSI) for police officers and firefighters who suffered a catastrophic injury in the line of duty. Catastrophic injuries — which range from hearing loss to paralysis — are defined as being a level of severity that result in the loss of an officer’s ability to maintain the certifications required by the state of Idaho, the officer’s respective department, or both.

Eligible public safety officers could receive a one-time injury benefit of $500,000 and an ongoing annual benefit no less than $75,000 a year with future adjustments every four years under this benefit category.

The amendment to this legislation — which passed unanimously in the House and the Senate — specifies this same monetary benefit will go toward the surviving spouse or, in the event there is no surviving spouse, the dependent children of a public safety officer who died in the line of duty from catastrophic injury.

Surviving families will be eligible for the new benefit if their spouse passed in the line of duty after July 1, 2021, when the previous law went into effect and — as was the case with the previous legislation — this new benefit will be funded through employees paying into the PERSI system an extra $110 per year. In what is a continuation of the existing death benefit framework, employers will pay for the first $100,000 of the officer’s benefit.

Ada County Sheriff Matt Clifford said there was a misstep with the previous legislation in not seeing that the changes wouldn’t apply to safety officers killed in the line of duty, an occurrence that is a rarity in the state of Idaho.

Following the deaths in Coeur d’Alene and discussion regarding the family of Bolter, however, Clifford said the Professional Firefighters of Idaho “took the reins” on the legislative changes in conjunction with the Idaho Fraternal Order of Police.

With the gaps of the past law now addressed, Clifford said the benefit, rather than being viewed as an “insurance policy,” is better understood as providing peace of mind for affected families.

“It’s peace of mind for … the deputy to say ‘if God forbid the worst happens, at least I know that my family’s taken care of,’” Clifford said. “The sacrifice I made for my community, at least some of that benefit gets passed to them.”

Josh Hoston, an engineer with the Coeur d’Alene Fire Department, said the changes mean sacrifices in the line of duty receive the same level of appreciation from the state.

“It’s time for the state to show appreciation and we will bear that cost ourselves,” Hoston said, in reference to the PERSI funding mechanism. “That’s what we do for families that give us everything.”

Royce McCandless is the Statehouse reporter and covers Idaho politics. You can email him at [rmccandless@idahopress.com](mailto:rmccandless@idahopress.com).
